**Proposition 3 Summary (November 3, 2026 Ballot)**

**Background**
- It is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment. It needed 874,641 valid signatures and made the ballot on June 10, 2026.
- Voters first approved these higher top-bracket rates in 2012 through Proposition 30. Proposition 55 later extended them through 2030. Under current law, the top rate drops back to 9.3% in 2031.
- Other titles include "High-Income Tax" and "The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026."

**What it does**
- Makes permanent the 10.3%, 11.3%, and 12.3% rates for the highest-income taxpayers.
- Keeps rates for lower-income taxpayers unchanged. The guide doesn't specify the income cutoffs.
- **Yes vote:** keeps those rates permanently, with education money split 89% to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
- **No vote:** current law stays, so the added rates lapse in 2031.

**Fiscal impact (Legislative Analyst's Office estimate)**
- Would keep an estimated $5B–$15B a year in state revenue that otherwise goes away after 2030.
- Annual totals shift because high earners' incomes are closely tied to economic and stock-market conditions.
- Roughly 40% goes to education (about $2B–$6B a year by my math), split into about $1.8B–$5.3B for K-12 and $0.2B–$0.7B for community colleges.
- Most of the remaining ~60% (roughly $3B–$9B by my math) would go to other state budget items and reserves.

**Arguments for**
- Backers see the higher rates as a vital investment for students, local communities, and educators.
- They claim the public is "demonstrably angry about income inequality."
- They argue that letting the rates lapse would give wealthy Californians a tax break.
- Supporters include the Yes on 3 campaign, California Teachers Association, California State PTA, California School Employees Association, CA School Nurses Organization, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA, California Democratic Party, and California Medical Association.

**Arguments against**
- Permanent rates could drive affluent residents and companies to relocate, potentially hurting jobs and growth.
- Opponents also say locking in the rates would complicate future policy changes.
- Opponents include the No on 3 campaign, California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, and Reform California.
- The guide refers readers to a separate endorsement table for additional groups.

**Accountability, spending, and unknowns**
- **Spending:** Only the education share (about 40%, split 89/11) is specified. The rest is described only broadly, as general state budget items and reserves. The guide doesn't say how much, if any, goes to health care, even though the title references it.
- **Accountability:** The guide describes no audits, oversight bodies, or reporting requirements. It only links Secretary of State campaign-finance tools.
- **Volatility:** Yearly amounts could land anywhere in the $5B–$15B estimate range.
- **Unquantified claims:** The guide gives no estimate of how many residents or businesses might leave. It also lists recent polls without reporting their findings.
- **Results:** The certified results fields are blank in this text, so no vote totals appear.

I can't reproduce the full text verbatim, so here is a summary of each argument and rebuttal with their specific claims. The complete text is in the [Print PDF](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3.pdf).

**Title and caption**
- The only title-level wording on this page is the caption: "PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES." It is followed by the designation "INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT."
- The official ballot label and the Official Title and Summary are not included in this content.

**Argument in favor (Yes side)**
- **No new tax:** Says the measure keeps current rates on the top 2% of earners, which they have paid for 15 years. Without it, millionaires and billionaires would get a large tax cut.
- **Cuts if it fails:** Says cuts of "billions" would hit about 8 million students, including layoffs of teachers and bigger classes. Also warns of risks to Medi-Cal and to preventive care and affordable medications.
- **Accountability:** Says constitutional protections keep funds with local schools, so state officials can't redirect them, and no money can go to bureaucracy or overhead. Cites annual independent audits, district spending posted online, and criminal penalties for officials who misuse funds.
- **Medi-Cal:** Says the school guarantee "frees up billions" that would go toward Medi-Cal for kids, older adults, and families.
- **Past results:** Says revenue has helped fund school lunches, smaller classes, counselors for mental health, children's healthcare, and Medi-Cal. It has also added to the Rainy Day Fund to limit cuts in downturns.
- **Support:** Lists nine groups, including the California Teachers Association, California Federation of Teachers, California Nurses Association, and California State PTA. Signed by David Goldberg (CTA), Katie Nilsson, RN (California School Nurses Organization), and Jodi Hicks (Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California).

**Argument against (No side)**
- **"Temporary" taxes:** Says voters were told the higher income taxes would last seven years to cover a deficit. They were then extended 12 more years on a promise to fix problems politicians created. Now they want them permanent.
- **Cost of living:** Says high income, sales, and gas taxes (the highest of all 50 states) partly explain California's top-ranked cost of living. Also cites the nation's priciest gas and higher insurance, utility, food, and housing costs.
- **Other taxes:** Says politicians are also pursuing taxes on health insurance and software and are "considering" a "jobs" tax.
- **Spending:** Says government spending rose $150 billion (more than 2.5X) after the temporary increases passed, while schools, infrastructure, and public safety deteriorated.
- **Budget swing:** A $100 billion surplus became a $30 billion deficit in three years.
- **Waste:** Cites $100 billion on a "train to nowhere," $37 billion on homeless programs it says don't work, and $31 billion on unemployment fraud.
- **Growth:** Says the population hardly grew over ten years while spending more than doubled. Also cites over 2,000 local tax hikes in the last ten years.
- **Signed by:** Robert Gutierrez (California Taxpayers Association), Robert Rivinius (Family Business Association of California), and Julian Canete (California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce).

**Rebuttal to the argument in favor (No side)**
- Says the 2012 promise was for temporary income taxes, and that making them permanent still counts as a tax increase.
- Calls it the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history," costing "up to $15 billion every year."
- Says taxpayers have carried those higher taxes for 16 years (the Yes side says 15).
- Says the measure does nothing about waste or fraud. Also cites the surplus-to-deficit claim, argues spending rather than revenue is the problem, and says population grew less than 2% in a decade while spending doubled.
- **Signed by:** Jon Coupal (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association), Carlos Solorzano (Hispanic Chambers of Commerce of San Francisco), and Clint Olivier (Central Valley Business Federation).

**Rebuttal to the argument against (Yes side)**
- Says the measure keeps the top 2% rates and that couples earning more than $740,000 would keep paying their current rates.
- Says without it, the wealthy would get a large tax cut and everyone else would cover the cost.
- Lists consequences of failure without dollar amounts: job losses for teachers and staff, fewer counselors, reduced support for Medi-Cal, children's healthcare, and clinics, and less money for firefighters, emergency services, and wildfire protection.
- Accountability: money goes directly to school districts and community colleges. "Not one penny may be spent on bureaucracy or administrative overhead." Also cites annual independent audits, district spending posted online, and criminal penalties for misuse.
- Says the school guarantee also lets the state fund Medi-Cal, children's healthcare, firefighters, and wildfire protection.
- **Signed by:** Jeff Freitas (California Federation of Teachers), Darrell Roberts (California Professional Firefighters), and Adam Weinberger (California School Employees Association).

**Points to note**
- **Conflicting durations:** The existing tax is described as 15 years (Yes argument and rebuttal), 16 years (No rebuttal), and as a seven-year term plus a 12-year extension (No argument).
- **Core dispute:** The Yes side says the measure keeps current rates and raises no taxes. The No side says the rates were meant to be temporary, so making them permanent is an increase.
- **Figures:** The only annual cost estimate is the No side's "up to $15 billion." The Yes side speaks of "billions" in cuts without specific amounts. None of the figures is sourced in these texts.
- **Opinions:** The page notes these are the authors' opinions and that no government body has verified them.

**Background**
- Among state taxes, the income tax raises the most. It covers most General Fund spending, and that fund pays for most public services.

- Planned General Fund spending this year is "about $250 billion." About half goes to schools, community colleges, and public universities. The State Constitution sets a floor for school and community college funding.

- Annual revenue would swing considerably, since much of it depends on income that tracks the stock market.

- Schools and community colleges would get "roughly 40 percent" of the money, and the remainder would go to "other state programs."
- A portion would go into budget reserves that the state could tap when revenues fall.

- **Yes:** 58%
- **No:** About 40%. The October figure is only given as "four in 10"; the exact 40% comes from September.
- **Undecided:** Not reported.

- **Party:** Majorities of Democrats and independents favor it, while most Republicans oppose it. No percentages given.

- **Age:** 73% yes among ages 18–34.
- **Renters:** 69% yes.
- **Region:** Majority support in every region. The Central Valley is nearly split, 51% yes to 48% no.

**Change over time**
- No change. PPIC's September survey showed identical results: 58% yes, 40% no.
- According to the same poll, support for a billionaire wealth tax "collapses," but the article gives no figures.

**Supporters**
- **California Teachers Association:** Has contributed $58.3 million, roughly 87% of the campaign's total funding. It warns that defeat would immediately reduce school and community college funding by 15%, possibly costing one in six educators their jobs. It insists "Prop. 3 will not raise taxes on anyone," saying the measure simply continues the existing tax on couples above $740,000 a year.

**Opponents**
- **California Taxpayers Association (David Kline):** Calls it an "unnecessary tax increase" that would raise living costs. He objects to writing the tax into the constitution years before its 2031 start. He says the fiscal emergency behind the temporary rates has ended, citing revenue gains and record school spending. He says the yes side's spending makes the fight "an uphill battle."
- **Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association:** Tells voters to say no in its published voter guide. It says the 2012 rates were presented as temporary "for the schools" and that these rate hikes "should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases."
- **Sonja Shaw (Republican-backed candidate for state schools chief):** Responds "Heck no." She says families are under strain, this is a bad moment for tax hikes, and the state needs accountability, not "a deeper slush fund for Sacramento insiders."

**Expert commentary**
- None. The article quotes no independent economists, academics, or analysts. Every quoted voice is an advocate, a union, or a candidate, and the PPIC numbers are reported without analysis.

Voters decide Prop 3 today (Nov. 3), so none of these results report an outcome. Key points:

- **Basics:** Voters first approved the top-bracket rates in 2012 under Prop 30 and extended them in 2016 through Prop 55. They are scheduled to lapse in 2031, and without the measure the top bracket reverts to 9.3%.
- **Rates and cutoffs:** Top rates run from 10.3% to 12.3%, and adding the state's 1% mental-health surcharge on income over $1 million lifts the combined top rate to 13.3%. The sources disagree on cutoffs. CalMatters' explainer lists $360,000 and $721,000 for individuals, while the Secretary of State's ballot summary uses $371,000 for individuals, adjusted annually for inflation, and another CalMatters article gives $743,000 for couples.
- **Revenue:** Collections typically run about $5–15 billion a year, roughly 3–10% of overall K-12 spending. Roughly 89% of proceeds would flow to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges, and any surplus to public health care.
- **Volatility:** The only volatility point I found is from a Kabateck Strategies explainer: receipts from top brackets can shrink sharply in downturns, even with high headline rates.
- **Timing dispute:** The same explainer says a defeat wouldn't immediately shrink revenue through 2027. Backers warn that failure could cost schools up to $15 billion a year and bring layoffs and cuts. The two may reflect different timing, since current rates run through 2030.
- **Supporters:** Spur, which urges a yes vote, points to over $119 billion raised for schools and health care and notes no evidence that high earners have left the state.
- **Opponents:** The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association objects that a permanent tax would betray an earlier pledge and could harm businesses, and it argues the 13.3% rate is too steep for small firms that file individually. Critics worry wealthy residents might move to lower-tax states and drain jobs and tax receipts from the state.
- **Budget view:** The California Budget & Policy Center, which makes the case for approval, contends the measure would leave rates unchanged and simply erase the sunset.
- **Gaps:** None of the results mention Proposition 98 or offer an economist's estimate of revenue volatility or stock-market exposure, and most are explainers or advocacy pieces. I found no 40% figure for Prop 3. The only "40" in the results is Prop 40, the billionaire tax, a separate wealth-tax initiative that would charge a one-time 5% levy on net worth. A follow-up on the Legislative Analyst's fiscal analysis would be the logical next search for economist-style estimates.

Here's a brief rundown of what the sources show about the 2012 Prop 30 measure:

- **Rauh and Shyu (2022):** Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu's analysis of California income tax filings from 2000 to 2019 finds that high earners' departures rose sharply around Prop 30 and the 2017 federal tax overhaul (TCJA), and movers with high incomes have consistently gravitated toward no-income-tax states since 2012.
- **2019 NBER study:** Work published by the NBER in 2019 documented a significant drop in taxable income and a significant rise in out-of-state moves among affected taxpayers. Departures and stayers' behavioral changes together offset about 45% of the revenue Prop 30 was expected to bring in during year one, and roughly 61% by year two.
- **Magnitudes:** Departures among affected high earners climbed about 42% above pre-Prop 30 levels, rising to 48% for those who would have faced the new top bracket three years running. More than 1.7% of the affected group exited the state in the measure's year.
- **Follow-up work:** A follow-up paper that builds on Rauh and Shyu adds taxable-income and revenue effects, and a summary on Edward Conard's blog says Southern California accounted for a larger share of out-of-state exits during the Prop 30 episode (the excerpt doesn't identify the authors).
- **Revenue effects:** A CalMatters commentary links the post-Prop 30 jump in out-migration and behavioral shifts to lower net state revenue, while a California Senate committee background paper explains that arrivals at the same income level don't fully make up for the tax owed by departing high earners.
- **Older counterpoint:** A 2012 Stanford–Princeton analysis, released about two weeks before the Prop 30 vote, concluded that the 2005 tax increase on high earners didn't drive wealthy residents away, putting migration at no more than 1.2% of yearly changes in the millionaire population. It predates Prop 30 and studies a different tax, so it isn't direct evidence on the measure.

- The ~$3.8 billion figure from the Rauh–Shyu work describes 2017 (TCJA), not Prop 30.
- A separate 2022 initiative, also numbered Prop 30, asked voters to approve a tax on income above $2 million for zero-emission vehicles and wildfire prevention.

**Author:** Dan Walters, opinion columnist for CalMatters, a nonprofit, nonpartisan newsroom. Published October 27, 2019, so its figures reflect that period.

**Argument:** California depends heavily on a small group of high earners for income tax revenue. Walters suggests that as taxes on them rise, some move to lower-tax states like Nevada, which can shrink state revenue.

**Evidence on departures:**
- **Anecdotes:** Gilbert Hyatt left Southern California for Las Vegas, and the state spent nearly three decades pursuing his taxes (no source given). A Wall Street Journal article from about two years earlier reported Michael and Nora Lacey's $31.1 million purchase of a former Steve Wynn estate on Lake Tahoe, which they made their official Nevada residence. The Tax Foundation projected that Raiders quarterback Derek Carr would avoid paying California $3.2 million annually by playing in Nevada.
- **Main study (an SSRN paper):** Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu found that high-income departures and "behavioral responses" rose noticeably after Proposition 30 (2012) raised income taxes on high earners, reducing net state revenue.

**Revenue effects:**
- Personal income taxes supply over two-thirds of the general fund, and about half of that comes from the top 1% (no source cited). Walters says "a few thousand" high earners pay "tens of billions of tax dollars" a year, funding schools, colleges, welfare, and prisons for roughly 40 million Californians.
- He flags "volatility": revenues surge in booms and drop in downturns.
- Proposition 30's increase was supposed to expire after a few years, but Proposition 55 (2016) pushed the end date to 2030. The 2017 federal tax law caps state and local deductions. A proposed 2020 ballot measure from education advocates would raise income taxes on high earners again, which he says could be "still another incentive" to leave.
- Jerry Brown, presenting his final budget in 2019, warned: "People with higher incomes pay a lot more money, and some of them may be tempted to leave."

**Caveats and counterarguments:**
- Walters acknowledges the individual cases are "anecdotal accounts" and says the study "provides new fuel for debate" rather than settling the question.
- He calls the state's dependence on top earners an "indisputable fact," but his flight evidence rests mainly on anecdotes and one study.
- Carr's $3.2 million is a projection, and his "back-loaded" contract shifts most pay to after the team moves. The Laceys' move would shield "at least some" of their income from California.
- The column offers no opposing arguments, no count of departures, no dollar estimate of the revenue lost, and no discussion of other reasons people move.

- **Title:** "Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California"
- **Authors:** Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu
- **Journal:** *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy*, vol. 16, no. 1 (February 2024), pp. 34–86. DOI: 10.1257/pol.20200500

**Condensed abstract**
- **Setup:** The authors use "administrative data" to study Proposition 30, described as "a 2012 measure that increased California marginal tax rates by up to 3 percentage points for high-income households."
- **Windfall offset:** Behavioral responses "eroded 45.2 percent of state windfall tax revenues within the first year" and "60.9 percent within 2 years." In other words, about 45% of the windfall was offset after one year and about 61% after two.
- **Departures:** Measured "relative to baseline departure rates," departures added "an additional 0.8 percent of the residential tax base that landed in the top bracket left California in 2013."
- **Departures vs. reported income:** The abstract says the erosion was "driven largely by the intensive margin." Because the elasticity is measured only among those who remained, this points to reduced reported income as the main channel, with departures playing a smaller role. The abstract does not quantify the split.
- **Elasticity:** Using "matched out-of-state taxpayers as controls," the authors estimate "an income elasticity with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5–3.2 for high earners who stayed." In plain terms, a 1% change in the share of marginal income kept after tax goes with roughly a 2.5–3.2% change in income among those who stayed.

**Bottom line:** Behavioral responses offset a large share of the windfall, and most of that offset came from reduced reported income rather than people leaving the state.

**Source:** CalMatters staff explainer, republished by KPBS. Published Sept. 23, 2026; updated Oct. 20, 2026.

**What Prop 3 does**
- Would make permanent an income tax on high earners that dates to 2012 and is otherwise set to end in 2031.
- The ballot text calls it an "initiative constitutional amendment" and describes it as making a "temporary tax increase on high-income earners" permanent.

**Rates and thresholds**
- 10.3% on income above $360,000
- 12.3% on income above $721,000
- Income in between is taxed at graduated rates. The article doesn't list those intermediate rates.
- Discrepancy: The ballot text sets the threshold at "over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation)." The article doesn't reconcile this with its $360,000 and $721,000 figures.

**Revenue**
- Usually generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year.
- The ballot's fiscal summary frames the measure as sustaining that revenue, which would otherwise end in 2031.

**Allocation**
- 89% to public K-12 schools
- 11% to community colleges
- Any excess to public health care. The article doesn't explain how excess is determined.
- Reserves and other uses: not mentioned.

**Accountability and audits**
- The article doesn't describe any accountability, oversight, or audit provisions.

**Supporters**
- *Argument:* The revenue is essential for schools. Supporters warn that if voters reject Prop 3, "the loss of up to $15 billion a year for schools" would likely bring layoffs, program reductions and other cuts.
- *Endorsements:* California Teachers Association, California School Employees Association, California State PTA, California Democratic Party, California Medical Association.

**Opponents**
- *Argument:* Opponents say the state already has "some of the highest income taxes in the country." They warn wealthier residents could relocate to lower-tax states, draining jobs and tax income from California.
- *Endorsements:* California Taxpayers Association, Reform California.

**Notes**
- The article names organizations but no individual officials.

**Bottom line:** Election day is today (Nov. 3, 2026), so none of these results report an outcome, and I found no dedicated fact-check outlet. The "40%" figure means different things in different sources, and I found no "15%" figure.

**If Prop 3 fails**
- Without the extension, roughly $5B–$15B a year in receipts would fall away. The LAO notes that swings in the yearly take track stock-market-linked income.
- The top rates lapse after tax year 2030, so revenue effects would not begin until 2031. Some outlets put the expiration in 2031.
- In the near term, General Fund money would have to close the gap in school funding.
- The California Budget & Policy Center (CBPC) projects the school guarantee would fall by roughly 40% of the lost revenue, compared with an extension. Spur flags possible erosion of the school minimum over time, tied to formula choice, the economy and legislative action.
- Backers warn a failure could mean job cuts and service reductions. Critics argue the tax could push wealthy residents out of state, draining jobs and tax receipts.

- **"40%":** The LAO puts the school share at roughly 40% of the measure's money, with the remainder flowing to other programs and some portion held in reserves. - **"$15B for schools":** Backers' $15B-a-year school figure is the top of the total revenue range. The LAO's 40% school share implies a long-run school loss nearer $2B–$6B (my arithmetic). My reading is that the $15B figure is closer to the near-term backfill need than to the long-run loss. The sources also diverge: CalMatters' 89% K-12 / 11% community college split implies most revenue goes to education, while the school guarantee is partly met with this money, so General Fund money is available for other priorities.
- **"15%":** I found no 15% figure. The nearest figure is CalMatters' 3%–10% share of overall K-12 spending.
- **CTA:** The CTA is the measure's sponsor. Its $33.3M of the $49.3M in top yes-side contributions makes it the largest of the top donors, and opposition committees had not reached $1M.

**Caveats:** GrowSF's page is written as a Yes-side guide, and CBPC's headline leans toward approval, so treat their figures as advocacy-leaning. The LAO is nonpartisan.

**Ballot label:** "Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes." "Initiative Constitutional Amendment."

**Summary**
- "Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation)."
- "Allocates tax revenues to public education."

**Fiscal impact:** "Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue" "by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031."

**Key numbers**
- **Income threshold:** people earning above $371,000, indexed to inflation each year.
- **Revenue preserved:** between $5 billion and $15 billion a year from state income taxes.
- **Timing:** the increase has been in effect since 2012 and would otherwise end in 2031.
- **Not specified:** no tax rate schedule or allocation percentage appears. The page only says revenue goes to education.

- Opens with "PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES."
- Says it "prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires" by keeping in place rates that "the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years."
- Claims it "requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms."
- Ends by urging a yes vote.

**Against (No)**
- Says Californians "already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes" and face the highest living costs.

content.content:
**Basics**
- The measure would make permanent a state income tax on high earners. Voters first approved it in 2012 as a short-term measure to cushion schools against the Great Recession, then extended it in 2016. It expires in 2031, and this is its third ballot appearance.
- It would apply to individuals earning above $371,000 and couples earning above $743,000 a year.
- The top bracket stays at 12.3%. Add the state's extra 1% on income above $1 million (which supports mental health programs), and the combined rate is 13.3%. The article, citing the Tax Foundation, calls that the nation's highest.
- Annual revenue has ranged from $5 billion to $15 billion, rising and falling with stock prices, interest rates and other drivers of top earners' income.

**Revenue and allocation**
- Most money would run through Proposition 98, which earmarks 40% of state budget dollars for K-12 and community colleges. Of that, 89% would reach K-12 and 11% would reach community colleges.
- Any amount above a set level would go into a rainy day fund.
- The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) says the measure would indirectly support health care and other state services by freeing up money that would otherwise go to schools.
- In strong revenue years, the tax would supply about 15% of K-12 education spending. The article gives no figure for leaner years.
- Goldberg warns that without the measure, as many as 50,000 teachers could be laid off, along with other cuts.

**Prop. 40 and possible interaction**
- Both measures are on the Nov. 3 ballot. Prop. 40 imposes a 5% levy on assets above $1 billion, sending 90% of its money to healthcare and splitting the rest among schools, food aid and other services.
- Prop. 3 taxes income, while Prop. 40 taxes assets.
- The teachers union opposes Prop. 40, saying schools would get too little of its money. David Goldberg adds: "We're not campaigning against Prop. 40. We're just prioritizing Prop. 3."
- The article doesn't say whether the two would conflict or interact if both pass.

**Supporters**
- David Goldberg, who leads the California Teachers Association, says: "It's only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it's vital for our schools."
- The union gathered thousands of signatures to qualify the measure and sent members to canvass over 200,000 doors. Goldberg called the drive "one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet."
- Placing the measure on the ballot more than four years before expiration gives schools time to plan budgets, Goldberg said.
- Rob Manwaring of Children Now links California's high student-teacher ratios to its achievement gap: "Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren't getting it."

**Opponents**
- Susan Shelley, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association's vice president, doubts schools need additional funding, citing recent state investments and falling enrollment. She asks: "Does this mean we need fewer teachers?"
- She says some districts have labor contracts they can't afford and calls the situation "not sustainable."
- She notes California already has the nation's steepest income tax on individuals (13.3%). She warns more taxes would push wealthy residents and their wealth out of state, hurting revenue disproportionately.

**Money and polling**
- The union and other groups have raised over $40 million for Prop. 3. Opponents, including taxpayer groups, have raised just $5,500.
- A September PPIC poll found 58% of likely voters planned to back the measure. Support was 82% among Democrats and 18% among Republicans.

**Caveats and analysis**
- Enrollment has fallen by over 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. The article ties this to fewer children, lower immigration and high living costs. Yet it also cites National Center for Education Statistics data showing about 22 students per teacher in 2022–23, versus a 15:1 national average and just over 11:1 in New York. The article leaves that tension unresolved.
- The article pairs Shelley's warning with LAO data showing the wealthiest 2% of earners pay roughly half of state income taxes. It doesn't assess whether high earners would actually leave.
- Health care funding is indirect, and the article gives no dollar figure for it, unlike Prop. 40's 90% healthcare share.
- Manwaring also warns that federal cuts and a possible downturn could strain budgets: "No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets."
- The article reads the poll as giving Prop. 3 the advantage. However, it cites only one September survey and gives no figures for opposition or undecided voters.

**Source:** LAO, "Initial Comments on the Governor's May Revision" (May 18, 2026), analyzing the May 14, 2026 proposal.

**1. 2026-27 budget condition**
- **No surplus.** The LAO says the plan meets the constitutional balance requirement, ending 2026-27 with a $4.5 billion Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties (SFEU) balance.
- **Structural deficit: $14 billion,** per the administration.
- **Reserves:** nearly $20 billion in general-purpose reserves, including about $15 billion in the Budget Stabilization Account (BSA).
- **Reliance:** roughly $20 billion in BSA withdrawals and suspended deposits (many adopted in prior budgets), plus about $4 billion in new settle-up borrowing.

**2. Structural deficits, 2027-28 and beyond**
- Roughly **$10 billion per year** through 2029-30 (the last year the text cites), per administration estimates. Year-by-year figures appear only in Figure 3.
- The LAO's own revenue estimates show a nearly identical gap.
- This roughly halves the $20 billion to $30 billion annual gaps projected in January.

**3. LAO view on volatile high-income and capital-gains revenue**
- The LAO ties the income tax surge (personal income tax up nearly 50% in three years) to AI and stock market enthusiasm.
- It argues booms are when the state should strengthen its finances, yet the May Revision draws reserves down.
- Revenue relies heavily on high earners, so it can swing sharply.
- The outlook rests heavily on stock valuations near dot-com peak levels, and such rallies usually end in sharp reversals.
- After the relatively mild 2022 market declines, income tax revenue for 2022-23 and 2023-24 came in $65 billion below Budget Act estimates. A dot-com-style bust could create a revenue shortfall of roughly $100 billion.
- The only capital gains reference is a $4.6 billion mandatory Proposition 98 Reserve deposit, triggered by higher capital gains revenue.
- The LAO sees no real surplus to protect. The proposed $9.7 billion TSHA deposit in 2026-27, withdrawn in 2027-28, effectively leans on 2026-27 money to shore up 2027-28.
- Recommendations include a $20 billion discretionary BSA deposit this year and redirecting the TSHA transfer.

**4. High-income tax rates expiring in 2031**
- Not addressed. The page's only tax expiration is the managed care organization (MCO) tax, scheduled to end at the close of 2026.

**5. Proposition 98 effects**
- The minimum requirement rises $6.4 billion across 2024-25 through 2026-27 versus January, absorbing part of the revenue gain.
- Freed-up funds: about $3.8 billion from lower baseline school formula costs, $1.6 billion from scaling back a January funding delay, and $807 million in unspent prior-year funds.
- A $6.2 billion reserve deposit ($4.6 billion mandatory, $1.6 billion discretionary) lifts the Prop 98 Reserve to $10.3 billion, or 8.3% of the 2026-27 requirement.
- $6.9 billion in added funding for schools and colleges, on top of $10.9 billion from January.
- The $4 billion settle-up frees up budget room now by funding 2025-26 below the constitutional level (January's plan had nearly $6 billion). The LAO sees merit as a hedge against revenue drops but treats it as borrowing. If 2025-26 revenues meet or beat forecasts, the state owes $4 billion later, so the LAO recommends setting aside $4 billion now.

**Caveat:** The page cites a $14 billion 2026-27 structural deficit but elsewhere says roughly $10 billion annually from 2026-27 onward, without reconciling the two.
